scores.evidence: Before acting, the handler re-fetches the object from Stripe, because webhook order isn't guaranteed.
scores.rationale: Claims about SQS at-least-once delivery, Stripe idempotency keys, webhook ordering, Postgres SEQUENCE gaps, RLS, Object Lock and SAQ-A scope are all accurate, including the subtle areas (partitioned unique keys, deferrable balance triggers, ON CONFLICT RETURNING semantics).

scores.evidence: This plan assumes (A). If you meant (B), the core still holds, but tenant isolation becomes the top driver
scores.rationale: Resolves the request's central ambiguity explicitly, covers every core billing capability, excludes scope with stated reasons and triggers, and the staged 5-7 month build with a week-1 build-vs-buy gate is credibly achievable.

scores.evidence: jobs are queued in the same transaction as the business change that triggers them. That gives you a transactional outbox
scores.rationale: Single writer per table, module ownership enforced by lint rules, idempotency and consistency decisions applied uniformly across flows, and no internal contradictions; cross-cutting identity and error propagation are handled the same way everywhere.

scores.evidence: Shadow differences for 1 real cycle: 100% explained, 0 unexplained above $0.01.
scores.rationale: The riskiest assumptions (volume S1, Stripe Tax S2, legacy parity S3, finance rules S4) are spiked in weeks 1-3 with time boxes and 'would change the plan' clauses, golden invoices and shadow cycles gate cutover, and ledger-balance and reconciliation checks continue in production.

scores.evidence: Every fact below about your stack, team, volumes, and current billing is an assumption. All of them are listed in Section 5
scores.rationale: Each assumption carries an impact-if-wrong and a validation method with a date, targets are labeled 'assumed, confirm with finance', and no invented specifics are presented as fact.

scores.evidence: the worker crashes after committing but before deleting the message. SQS redelivers it after the visibility timeout
scores.rationale: Covers duplicates, out-of-order webhooks, partial failures mid-transaction, tax-provider outages, SCA, late usage, forged usage, insider fraud and corruption detection (ledger imbalance alarm, restore drills) with concrete detection and recovery; only explicit chargeback/refund flows are left to reconciliation.

scores.evidence: document rollback as redeploying the previous image tag ... a rollback has been done once
scores.rationale: Deployment, rehearsed rollback, expand/contract migrations, symptom-based alerts each linked to a runbook, named ownership split between engineering and finance, and a month-end checklist all sized to a 4-5 person team.

scores.evidence: The main cost driver is Stripe fees (card processing plus per-transaction Stripe Tax fees), not infrastructure.
scores.rationale: Identifies the dominant cost driver correctly, grounds the ~$2.5k-5k/month infrastructure range in named components, states the ~5-7 month build cost, weighs vendor percentage-of-volume fees in the build-vs-buy decision, and includes concrete controls.

scores.evidence: In practice, the first native invoice is that tenant's point of no return.
scores.rationale: Every key decision carries an explicit reversibility rating and revisit trigger, the hard ones (D1, D4, D5, D6, D12) get ADRs and early gates, vendor coupling is isolated behind TaxProvider/PaymentProvider interfaces, and points of no return are named.

scores.evidence: Not split into microservices, because no driver needs independent scaling apart from usage ingestion, and the queue already absorbs that.
scores.rationale: One modular deployable on one Postgres, no speculative infrastructure, each component justified against a driver, deferrals listed with triggers, and the plan even offers to cut itself by 70% if pricing turns out simple.

scores.evidence: Time box: 4 days. ... Would change the plan: a failure means producer-side pre-aggregation or moving raw events to S3 (D3)
scores.rationale: Tasks T0-T24 have locations, 'done when' criteria and an ordering justified by dependencies, next steps start today, and each spike states how disappointing results would change the plan.

checklist.evidence: Money is stored as integers in minor units (cents) ... Each line is rounded half-up to minor units, and the invoice total is the sum of the rounded lines.
Issued invoices are never edited; corrections are made only through credit notes. ... Every money movement is posted to an append-only, double-entry ledger
The job retries with the same key, Stripe returns the same PaymentIntent, and no second charge is made.
the product web app collects the card with Stripe Elements. Card data never reaches you. ... the status becomes requires_action
Tenant ID comes only from the token; RLS; negative tests on every portal endpoint in CI.
The next billing run bills quantity − billed_quantity as a "usage adjustment for <period>" line.
Price versions are immutable, so a price change always means a new prices row and existing subscriptions keep their old price.
an EU business with a VAT ID (reverse charge) ... a row per issuing entity in invoice_number_sequences, locked with SELECT … FOR UPDATE
retries on days 3/5/7 ... tenant admin notified on day 14, entitlement status restricted (read-only) on day 21, suspended on day 45
a daily job matches Stripe balance transactions against StripeClearing ... Finance owns reconciliation tickets.
Entitlements are pushed to the product and cached there ... If billing is down, tenants can still use the product
Build rating, invoicing, and ledger. Buy payments and tax (Stripe). ... off-the-shelf tools get rigid and costly (fees as a percentage of billed volume)

traps.evidence: Integer minor units for amounts; numeric(38,12) for unit prices; round half-up per line
A finalised invoice is never updated. Corrections are made through credit_notes.
the signature is verified, the raw event is stored in psp_webhook_events (unique on the Stripe event ID)
Storing card or bank data. Stripe holds it, which keeps you in the lightest PCI category (SAQ-A).
Postgres row-level security (RLS) as a second layer of defence ... negative tests on every portal endpoint in CI

note: An exemplary plan: technically precise on the hard billing problems (idempotency, immutability, metering, isolation), with early de-risking spikes, shadow-cycle validation, explicit assumptions and reversibility; only explicit chargeback/refund flows are notably thin.
